e.etymology: Mary and Ann, a pairing so common that it came to be written as one word. It was at its most popular in the United States in the 1940s.
namesakes: Mary Ann Summers (the farm girl on Gilligan's Island)

e.etymology: A pet form of Scott, a surname and first name that originally meant a Scot or a Gaelic speaker.
namesakes: Montgomery Scott (Scotty, chief engineer on Star Trek)
Scotty McCreery (country singer and American Idol winner)
Scotty Bowman (winningest coach in NHL history)

assoc.t: Scotty, Star Trek's engineer (Beam me up, Scotty)

e.etymology: From Arabic amin, trustworthy or faithful. Al-Amin, the trustworthy one, was a title of the Prophet Muhammad.
Spanish and Italian for rosary, from the title of the Virgin Mary as Our Lady of the Rosary. It is a girls' name in Spanish and a boys' name in Italian.
namesakes: Rosario Dawson (actress in Rent and Sin City)

e.etymology: From Arabic Amir with a long first vowel, the active participle of a verb meaning to be inhabited or to flourish. It is a different name from Amir, prince.
namesakes: Aamir Khan (Bollywood star of Lagaan and Dangal)

e.etymology: The Spanish word for flower, from Latin flos. It is also short for Florencia and part of compound names such as Flor de María.
A one-n spelling of Johanna, the Latin feminine of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. This spelling is used in Czech and across Latin America.

e.meaning: clearing of Cyne, an Old English name meaning royal
e.etymology: A respelling of Kinsley, an English place name and surname meaning the clearing (leah) of a man named Cyne, an Old English name that means royal. It is often glossed as king's meadow.
A modern American coinage, a variation on Braxton and Brixton with the x-and-ton sound of Paxton and Jaxton.
Invented by Sir Philip Sidney for his romance Arcadia in the late 1500s, perhaps with Greek pan, all, and meli, honey, in mind. Samuel Richardson's 1740 novel Pamela made it widely known.
namesakes: Pam Beesly (the receptionist on The Office)
Pam Grier (star of Foxy Brown and Jackie Brown)

e.etymology: The Irish form of Joan, taken from Anglo-Norman Jehanne in the Middle Ages and going back to Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious.
namesakes: Siobhan Roy (Shiv, the daughter in HBO's Succession)
e.note: The spelling gives no clue to the sound (shih-VAHN), so expect it to be misread.

e.etymology: The Russian form of Michael, from Hebrew Mikha'el, who is like God?, the name of the archangel.
namesakes: Mikhail Gorbachev (last leader of the Soviet Union)

e.meaning: riverbank; one who lived by a river
e.etymology: An English surname of Norman origin, from places in northern France called Rivieres, the riverbanks. As a first name it works as a surname-style form of River.
A modern American name with the sound of Josiah and Isaiah behind a Jaz- opening. A similar name, Jaaziah, belongs to a Levite in the Old Testament.
A modern American name without a single source. Some use it as a form of Kyran, from Irish Ciaran, little dark one; others build it from the Ky- of Kyrie and Kyle.
From the French phrase j'adore, I adore or I love it, written as one word. Many Americans know the phrase from Dior's perfume J'adore, launched in 1999.

assoc.t: j'adore, French for I adore or I love it

e.etymology: A spelling of Eliana, which in Hebrew means my God has answered and in Italian and Spanish descends from the Roman family name Aelianus.
A K spelling of the word clarity, from Latin claritas, clearness or brightness, the same root as Clara and Claire.
A modern blend of Audrey and Adriana.
Hebrew keren means horn and also ray of light. In the Bible Keren-happuch is one of Job's three daughters, and the short form is used in Israel and across Latin America.
e.note: Sounds almost the same as Karen, now slang for an entitled complainer.

e.etymology: An Irish surname, the anglicized form of O Duibhginn, descendant of Duibhgeann, a byname from dubh, black, and ceann, head.
In German an old name from hagan, enclosure, borne by the grim warrior Hagen in the Nibelungenlied. In Danish it is a form of Old Norse Hakon. It is also a German place name and surname.
namesakes: Tom Hagen (the consigliere in The Godfather)

e.etymology: Arabic Abd al-Rahman, servant of the Most Merciful. Al-Rahman is one of the names of God in the Quran, and a saying of the Prophet Muhammad counts this among the names God loves most.

e.meaning: noble (as a short form of Adelina)
e.etymology: A spelling of Alina, used across Central and Eastern Europe and usually explained as a short form of Adelina, from the Germanic element adal, noble.
A modern American coinage that puts a T in front of the -aelyn sound of Kaelyn, Raelyn and Jaelyn.
A Yiddish pet form of Sarah, Hebrew for princess, reflecting the Hasidic pronunciation Sura. The -y spelling is used mainly in Hasidic Jewish communities.
A name used mainly in Mexico and among Mexican Americans, made familiar by actress Nailea Norvind. Its source is uncertain; it is often linked to Arabic Naila, one who attains.
namesakes: Nailea Devora (YouTube and social media personality)

e.etymology: From Hawaiian alaka'i, to lead or guide, and as a noun a leader. The Alaka'i Swamp on Kauai is a high rainforest wilderness.
A modern feminine spelling of Jordan, the river of the Bible, from Hebrew Yarden, to flow down. Crusaders brought its water home for baptisms, which made Jordan a given name.

assoc.t: Jordan, Middle Eastern country and river (spelled Jordan)

e.etymology: In American use a modern name in the family of Samara, Amaya and Samiyah. Samaya is also a Sanskrit word for an appointed time or a vow.
A pet form of Hinda, a Yiddish name meaning hind, a female deer. It is used almost entirely in Hasidic Jewish communities.
e.note: Sounds the same as Hindi, the language of northern India.

e.etymology: The Spanish form of Nehemiah, Hebrew for Yahweh comforts. Nehemiah was the governor who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem after the exile in Babylon.
